newsitem.title: UGANDA: Uganda's Museveni hosts mini-summit on Zaire.
newsitem.headline: Uganda's Museveni hosts mini-summit on Zaire.

text.p: Ugandan President Yoweri Museveni on Friday met Rwandan military strongman Paul Kagame and Burundi ruler Pierre Buyoya to seek common ground on the refugee crisis in eastern Zaire and regional economic sanctions on Burundi.
Kagame, Rwanda's Tutsi vice-president and defence minister, arrived in Uganda on Thursday. Buyoya, also an ethnic Tutsi, arrived early on Friday.

"Kagame and Buyoya want to seek common ground on the refugee question. They want Museveni to use his influence to get their opinions on the matter listened to," a foreign ministry official said. "That is why they requested this meeting."
On Tuesday, Museveni said he wanted Buyoya removed and it was an insult for anyone to claim he backed the Burundian.
But at Entebbe Airport on Friday, Ugandan Foreign Minister Eriya Kategaye said: "Uganda recognises Buyoya as the de facto leader of Burundi and he is here in that capacity."
Buyoya was flown in a Ugandan army helicopter to a remote western town for his meeting with Museveni and Kagame.

Buyoya replaced Hutu president Sylvestre Ntibantunganya, who took the Burundian presidency after the 1993 murder of president Melchior Ndadaye, who had won presidential elections earlier in that year.
Ndadaye's death plunged Burundi into anarchy. Normalcy has not returned since.
East African states imposed economic and transport sanctions on Burundi six days after the July 25 coup. Uganda, Tanzania and Kenya have been the main players in maintaining sanctions.
Buyoya hoped he could persuade Museveni to convince regional leaders that a lifting of sanctions could help ordinary people in Burundi, African diplomats in Kampala said.
Buyoya and Kagame also wanted their positions on an intervention force in Zaire amplified for them by Museveni.
Kagame said on Wednesday he was suspicious of the need to link humanitarian aid for thousands of returning Hutu refugees to the presence of an international force in Rwanda.
"If humanitarian assistance is tied to a force, then I am right to be suspicious," he told a news conference.
Kagame, who is considered the most powerful man in the Rwandan government, said the return of thousands of Hutu refugees from eastern Zaire created the need for aid, not arms.
Burundi has said it wanted the intervention force to separate so-called genuine refugees from extremists.

The countries that have agreed to participate in the intervention force, originally intended to help feed refugees in eastern Zaire and help them return home, have called a meeting in Germany for Friday.
Kagame said he believed the number of refugees remaining in eastern Zaire -- which aid agencies and western governments say could be 500,000 or more -- had been exaggerated.
Around 35,000 Burundian Hutus who fled camps north of Uvira town in Zaire last month have returned to Burundi, most of them crossing into the troubled north west Cibitoke region.

But the influx has been overshadowed by the return home of Rwandan Hutus from camps around Goma in North Kivu between November 15 and 19. Some 700,000 Rwandan and Burundian refugees remain in Zaire according to U.N. refugee agency figures.
Around 150,000 people have died in the past three years in a civil war after Burundi's first elected Hutu president was killed in an attempted coup by Tutsi soldiers.
